subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Dark Patterns in UX
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Dark Patterns in UX.

hook.text: The unsubscribe button is grey, tiny, and buried in settings. The subscribe button is green, large, and centered.

buildup.text: Dark patterns are UX designs that trick users into actions they didn't intend.

discovery.text: Brignull cataloged types: roach motels, misdirection, forced continuity, and confirm-shaming.

twist.text: The EU and FTC now regulate dark patterns. Amazon was fined for making Prime cancellation require six clicks.

climax.text: When a website makes canceling harder than joining, it uses a dark pattern. Recognize the design and push through it.

punchline.text: If leaving is hard, they designed it that way.

quiz.question: What are dark patterns?
options: UX designs that trick users into unintended actions
Patterns used to improve website accessibility

details.summary: Dark patterns are user interface designs that deliberately trick users into actions they did not intend, such as hidden subscriptions, confusing opt-out flows, and misdirected clicks. They exploit cognitive biases for the company's benefit at user expense.
details.whyItMatters: Dark patterns erode consumer trust and are increasingly targeted by regulation. Recognizing these deceptive design techniques helps users protect themselves and pushes designers toward ethical alternatives that build long-term loyalty.
takeaways: Dark patterns exploit cognitive biases through deliberately confusing design
Common types include roach motels, trick questions, and forced continuity
Regulatory action against dark patterns is increasing globally

faq.question: What is the most common dark pattern on the internet?
faq.answer: Forced continuity, where free trials auto-convert to paid subscriptions with no clear cancellation path, is the most prevalent. Users sign up for free, forget to cancel, and are charged. The difficulty of canceling is deliberately engineered.

faq.question: Are dark patterns illegal?
faq.answer: Increasingly, yes. The EU, California, and other jurisdictions are passing laws against deceptive design. The FTC has taken enforcement action against companies using manipulative subscription flows and confusing consent mechanisms.
